title: Ground protection and environmental runoff
audience: Trainees, workers and owners of solar cleaning businesses who plan jobs and want to reduce cost, waste and callbacks without taking unsafe shortcuts.
learningOutcomes: Identify cost-reduction measures for a PV clean that keep the work inside its safety and scope limits.
Explain how ground protection and runoff control reduce both cost and environmental harm.
Apply a decision that trades a time-saving shortcut against the scope, the safety rules and the environmental rules.

Only part of the Wollondilly and Toowoomba sources has been confirmed.

instruction.heading: Cost reduction within the scope
instruction.body: Cleaning cost is driven by time, travel, materials, equipment, rework and callbacks. A solar clean reduces cost when the job is planned from the ground, when the array is inspected before work starts, when the scope is agreed in writing, and when the method uses only the approved products and equipment. Cost reduction does not mean taking roof access without approval, skipping the inspection, or using a stronger product to finish faster. Those shortcuts increase the risk of damage, incident and warranty dispute, which costs more than the time saved.

instruction.heading: Ground-based planning first
instruction.body: Where the array can be reached from the ground, or where a ground-based method is possible, plan that method first. Ground-based work avoids roof access and the costs of approval, equipment and supervision that roof access requires. Where the array is on a roof, record why a ground-based method is not possible, and do not treat roof access as the default.

instruction.heading: Ground protection
instruction.body: Ground protection means protecting the turf, soil, paths, cables, pits and garden beds from the damage that equipment and vehicles can cause. Place boards or mats where a ladder, a trolley or a vehicle will stand. Keep cables and hoses clear of walkways and off the ground where they can be trodden on. Damage to the ground is a cost, and it is also a hazard for trips and for underground services. The site controller decides where equipment may be placed.

instruction.heading: Runoff and stormwater
instruction.body: Wash water from a solar clean can carry detergent, dirt, bird droppings and any residue from the panel surface. NSW EPA guidance (dated January 2021) says the stormwater drain is for water only, and that chemicals should be kept in bunded, closed and labelled storage rather than tipped in the drain. A NSW council fact sheet (no date shown) states that polluted run-off reaching a drain or waterway is an offence under the NSW Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997, which can carry substantial penalties. For example, NSW EPA guidance (dated January 2021) asks for dedicated washdown areas that do not lead to stormwater drains, so runoff from a site without one should be held or collected as the job plan requires. In Queensland, a council page (no date shown) states that wastewater from pressure cleaning may not be let into kerbside channels or the stormwater network, and cites section 440ZG of the Environmental Protection Act 1994. Use the lowest water volume the method allows, use approved products only, and divert or collect the runoff as the job plan requires. Where runoff reaches a drain, record it, and report it under the site's procedure.

instruction.heading: Water and product use
instruction.body: Use only the water that the job needs. Leaving a hose running, flooding the array or using unfiltered water where the manufacturer does not allow it wastes water and can damage the array and its warranty. Use approved products at the labelled concentration, and do not increase the concentration to save time. Record the water and product used so that the cost and the environmental impact can be reviewed.

instruction.heading: Reducing callbacks
instruction.body: Callbacks cost money. A pre-clean inspection, a written scope, a record of the array condition before work, and an approved method all reduce callbacks because they show what was there before the clean and what was done. A record of the condition is the best protection against a later dispute about damage.

instruction.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instruction.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, environmental approval or authority to discharge wastewater, to work on the ground in a regulated area, or to access a roof.

procedure: Plan the job from the ground, and record whether a ground-based method can reach the array.
Agree the scope, the exclusions and the method in writing, and inspect the array before work starts.
Place ground protection where equipment, ladders or vehicles will stand, and keep cables and hoses clear of walkways.
Use the lowest water volume the method allows, and only approved products at the labelled concentration.
Keep wash water out of stormwater, and divert or collect it as the job plan requires.
Record the water and product used, the ground protection placed and any runoff observed.
Do not take a shortcut that breaches the scope, the safety rules or the environmental rules to save time.

workedExamples.situation: A worker plans to save time by leaving the hose running across the lawn and by using a product at double the labelled strength. The water runs toward a storm drain.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which parts of this plan must change, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: Both shortcuts must change. The hose must be used only for the water the job needs, and the runoff must be kept out of the drain. The product must be used at the labelled strength, because a higher strength increases the risk to the surface and the runoff. Record the plan change. Any runoff that reaches a drain must be recorded and reported.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks the cleaner to go on the roof to save time, although the array is reachable from a ground-level position.
workedExamples.reasoning: Plan the ground-based method first, because roof access adds approval, equipment and supervision costs and risk. Record why the ground-based method cannot reach the array, if that is the case, and do not treat roof access as the default. If roof access is needed, hold the job until approval, a safe access method and competent oversight are in place.

equipmentAndPpe: Low-volume approved applicator and a water measure
Approved product with its label and safety data sheet
Eye protection, gloves and footwear as specified in the job pack

commonErrors.error: Leaving a hose running to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the water the job needs, and turn the supply off between passes.

commonErrors.error: Increasing the product strength to finish faster.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the labelled concentration, and record the product used.

commonErrors.error: Taking roof access because it is quicker.
commonErrors.prevention: Plan the ground-based method first, and hold the job if approval is missing.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the array inspection to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the array condition before work, because the record protects against disputes.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Stormwater: NSW and Queensland sources are cited in the runoff section above.
Ground protection and the placement of equipment on site are set by the site controller.
Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, environmental approval or authority to discharge wastewater or to access a roof.

qualityStandard: The job is planned from the ground first, and any roof access is approved and recorded.
Ground protection is placed where equipment and vehicles stand.
Water and product use is recorded, and runoff is kept out of stormwater.
No shortcut is taken that breaches the scope, safety or environmental rules.
documentationEvidence: Ground-based method assessment and the reason for any roof access
Water and product use record with the labelled concentration
Runoff observation and the control applied
summary: Cost savings must stay inside the scope, the safety rules and the environmental rules.
Plan from the ground first, and protect the ground where equipment stands.
Keep runoff out of stormwater, and use only the water and product the job needs.
This lesson grants no environmental approval, wastewater discharge or roof-access authority.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which cost-reduction measure keeps the job inside its safety and scope limits?
options: Repeated roof access without approval from the owner or the body corporate
Using extra chemicals to speed up the wash on the roof, the frame and the rails
Cleaning without records of the work done on the site, the roof or the array
Choosing a ground-based method where the array is reachable from the ground

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should wash water from a solar clean go?
options: Kept out of stormwater, and controlled as the site plan requires
Into the stormwater drain at the kerb and the gutter below the house
Onto the neighbour's garden beds and lawn at the side of the house
Onto the roof and the gutters above the work area today

knowledgeChecks.question: Ground protection for a ground-mounted array means:
options: Digging trenches for the cables and the pipes at the site today
Protecting turf, soil and cables from equipment damage and vehicle traffic
Watering the ground with product to keep it damp all day long at the site
Walking on cables laid across the ground by the whole crew at the site

knowledgeChecks.question: Which action reduces callbacks without breaching the scope?
options: Skipping the pre-clean inspection to save time on the day for the client and the crew
Using a stronger product on all panels to get them clean quickly and well today
Recording the array condition before work and agreeing the scope in writing
Working faster on the roof to finish the job sooner each time and every week

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker wants to reduce water waste. Which action is consistent with this draft?
options: Leave the hose running while the crew takes a break for lunch and tea each day at the site
Use unfiltered water on all arrays regardless of the manufacturer's advice
Flood the array with water from the hose to rinse it fast and well on the day
Use the approved method with only the water the job needs, and keep runoff controlled
